section_summary: This section documents State Department monitoring of strategic-material exports to Japan and the Soviet Union, including ethyl fluid, molybdenum, Brazilian rubber, and possible arms sales. It also contains extensive lobbying material from the American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression, listing religious, civic, labor, peace, women’s, and China-aid groups supporting an embargo. The closing pages comprise a Woman’s Council covering letter and numerous petitions asking the President and Congress to end American trade that supported Japan’s war in China.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment concerning Ralph L. Harding’s letter on war-material sales to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene’s transmission of a letter from Ralph L. Harding concerning sales of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department thanks Roger Greene for his April 20 letter enclosing Ralph Harding's comments on war-material sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Letter quoting Representative Bruce Barton on a proposed embargo
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene
subfiles.to: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Calls attention to Bruce Barton’s statements about an embargo on war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene quotes Representative Bruce Barton as arguing that an embargo was an exceptionally serious step and that Congress should await a State Department recommendation. Greene believes Barton is mistaken about Sino-Japanese diplomatic relations and about embargoes commonly leading to war, but notes Barton’s confidence in Hull’s judgment.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Greene’s letter about Bruce Barton
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene’s confidential report of Representative Bruce Barton’s views.
subfiles.summary: Department thanks Greene for his April 5 confidential letter forwarding Bruce Barton's remarks on exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Report of no ethyl-fluid shipments in January or February
subfiles.from: J. Goux
subfiles.to: Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Reports that no relevant shipments were made during January and February and promises continuing reports.
subfiles.summary: Goux reports no ethyl-fluid shipments in January or February and promises reports each month.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of J. Goux’s ethyl-fluid report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: J. Goux
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report of no ethyl-fluid shipments to Japan or the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes Goux's report of no January or February shipments and expects future reports.

subfiles.title: Telephone report of a possible molybdenum sale to a Japanese concern
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green
subfiles.to: Department of State file
subfiles.about: Records Treasury information that A. S. Gaudine might sell 20,000 tons of molybdenum to a Japanese company.
subfiles.summary: Basil Harris told Green New York Customs reported an offer to sell 20,000 tons of molybdenum, apparently to Iwai and Company; Green will investigate.

subfiles.title: Investigation of A. S. Gaudine’s molybdenum inquiries
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, with addendum by Joseph C. Green
subfiles.to: Department of State file
subfiles.about: Records Gaudine’s denial of a reported molybdenum sale and the Department’s suspicions about his inquiries.
subfiles.summary: Gaudine denied owning or selling molybdenum but admitted visiting Climax and asking Customs about export restrictions; Yost thinks he investigated supplies for a foreign interest and was discouraged.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on reexports of Brazilian rubber
subfiles.from: Mr. Veatch
subfiles.to: Department of State file
subfiles.about: Reports trade information about Brazilian rubber allegedly imported for reexport to Japan and possibly handled by American brokers.
subfiles.summary: Viles reports Brazilian rubber reaching New York for reexport to Japan, tied to the Kansai Maru and Amtorg, naming possible dealers; recommends bringing the strategic-material policy to their attention.

subfiles.title: Request for Rubber Trade Association inquiry into the Frank B. Ross Company
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: A. L. Grant
subfiles.about: Asks the Rubber Trade Association to investigate reported Brazilian-rubber exports involving a member company.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks the Rubber Trade Association to examine whether the Frank B. Ross Company handled Brazilian rubber for Japan and eventual Soviet transshipment.

subfiles.title: Warning to Steinharter and Nordlinger about Brazilian-rubber reexports
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Steinharter and Nordlinger
subfiles.about: Warns the firm that reexporting Brazilian rubber to Japan or the Soviet Union would conflict with government policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department cites a report that the firm participated in sales of Brazilian rubber for export to Japan and possible transshipment to the Soviet Union. It encloses War and Navy Department policy releases and requests the firm’s full cooperation in avoiding such strategic-material transactions.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing lists of organizations supporting an embargo
subfiles.from: Roger S. Greene
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Forwards lists of local and national organizations supporting an embargo on war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene suggests Hamilton's staff examine lists of groups acting for an embargo, cities with committee branches and cooperating national organizations.

subfiles.title: Partial list of organizations supporting the embargo campaign
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Department of State
subfiles.about: Lists local religious, civic, peace, women’s, China-aid, and labor organizations supporting an embargo or related action.
subfiles.summary: The compilation records resolutions, petitions, letters, contributions, boycotts, and demonstrations by organizations across the United States. It includes churches and missionary societies, general civic groups, peace organizations, women’s associations, China-aid committees, and labor bodies. Several entries describe local efforts to halt scrap-iron shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cities containing branches of the ACNPJA
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Department of State
subfiles.about: Lists cities throughout the United States in which the committee maintained branches.
subfiles.summary: The list organizes branch locations by state, from Alabama and Arizona through Washington and Wisconsin. It demonstrates the geographic reach of the committee’s anti-export campaign.

subfiles.title: National organizations cooperating with the committee
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Department of State
subfiles.about: Identifies national organizations and contacts that cooperated with and supported the committee.
subfiles.summary: The document lists peace, church, educational, women’s, China-aid, and boycott organizations, together with named representatives and addresses. It provides a contact network for national coordination of the campaign.

subfiles.title: National and regional groups protesting aid to Japan or other aggressors
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and Department of State
subfiles.about: Lists national and regional religious, labor, peace, student, and professional bodies protesting aid to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: List of major church assemblies, women's groups, unions, student groups and regional embargo conferences protesting aid to Japan or other aggressors.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Greene’s organizational lists
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Greene’s lists of embargo supporters, committee branches, and cooperating national organizations.
subfiles.summary: Department acknowledges Greene's April 23 letter and its three categories of organizational material.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese arms and military supplies sold to Bolivia
subfiles.from: Bolivia (Jenkins)
subfiles.to: Department of State file
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report that a Japanese arms representative obtained a Bolivian government order.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 134: Mitsui Okura's Miyata won a Bolivian order for Japanese arms and military supplies in La Paz.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: “Embargo Opponent May be next President of U.S.A.”
subfiles.from: Japan (Grew)
subfiles.to: Department of State file
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Japan Times article concerning an American presidential prospect opposed to an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 4583: a March 1 Japan Times article 'Embargo Opponent May be next President of U.S.A.'

subfiles.title: Woman’s Council letter forwarding petitions against aid to Japan
subfiles.from: W. O. Tufts, Woman’s Council of the Washington Federation of Churches
subfiles.to: Franklin D. Roosevelt; referred to the Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards petitions opposing American support for Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: Woman's Council sends Roosevelt petitions condemning American aid to Japan's China war; a White House notation refers them to State.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for Japan, signed by W. O. Tufts
subfiles.from: W. O. Tufts
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Petitions the federal government to end American trade supporting Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: W. O. Tufts's petition condemns Japanese aggression and bombing, asking the President and Congress to stop shipments of raw materials, aircraft, scrap iron and oil.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for Japan, signed from 1635 Madison Street
subfiles.from: W. O. Tufts or another signer at 1635 Madison Street
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for practical measures to end American trade that facilitated Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Petition says American exports make the US a partner in destroying the Chinese people, invoking the Nine-Power Treaty, Kellogg Pact and Good Neighbor principle.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for Japan, signature unclear
subfiles.from: Unidentified petitioner
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests an end to exports and other traffic supporting Japanese aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: Petition, signature unclear, condemns bombing of Chinese cities and urges action by the President and Congress to end the trade.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for Japan, signed by W. O. Tufts
subfiles.from: W. O. Tufts
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges the government to stop American supplies from contributing to Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: W. O. Tufts's petition cites treaty violations, civilian attacks and destruction of foreign institutions, and lists scrap iron, oil, trucks and aircraft to be curtailed.

subfiles.title: Petition against American support for Japan representing 3,000 women
subfiles.from: Unidentified representative of 3,000 women
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Presents an anti-war-supply petition on behalf of a large group of women.
subfiles.summary: Petition says American trade enables Japan's invasion; a handwritten note says the signer represents 3,000 women.

subfiles.title: Petition from the Washington Lutheran Missionary Union
subfiles.from: Washington Lutheran Missionary Union, signed by John H. Rush
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests federal action to end American trade aiding Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Washington Lutheran Missionary Union petition links American materials to Japanese bombing and asks every practicable measure to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by F. E. Edington
subfiles.from: F. E. Edington
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks an end to American commerce supporting Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: F. E. Edington signs as a registered voter in Pennsylvania's First District, condemning exports used against the Chinese population.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by W. L. Darby
subfiles.from: W. L. Darby
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls upon federal authorities to halt American trade contributing to Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: W. L. Darby signs the standard petition condemning Japanese aggression and American complicity.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Gan R. Smi
subfiles.from: Gan R. Smi, name uncertain
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests measures to end American shipments used by Japan in China.
subfiles.summary: Petition signed by Gan R. Smi on military use of American aircraft, shells, scrap iron and oil, asking to end the traffic.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by J. A. Borre
subfiles.from: J. A. Borre
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Opposes American material support for Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: J. A. Borre's petition condemns bombing of Chinese civilians and destruction of schools and hospitals and asks federal authorities to halt the trade.

subfiles.title: Unsigned petition against American support for Japan
subfiles.from: Unidentified petitioner
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges action to terminate American trade supporting Japanese warfare in China.
subfiles.summary: Unsigned standard petition invoking treaty obligations, civilian suffering and American complicity through strategic exports.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Mabel V. Mercer
subfiles.from: Mabel V. Mercer, associated with Calvary Baptist Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American exports that aided Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Mabel Mercer signs the standard appeal, identifying Calvary Baptist Church.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Mrs. Ralph S. Hubbard
subfiles.from: Mrs. Ralph S. Hubbard, National City Christian Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests government action against American trade supporting Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Ralph Hubbard signs, identifying National City Christian Church and an Alexandria address.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Mrs. John L. Beale
subfiles.from: Mrs. John L. Beale, Church of the Pilgrims
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges termination of American material assistance to Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. John Beale signs the common petition, noting the Presbyterian Church of the Pilgrims.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Beretta C. Burton
subfiles.from: Beretta C. Burton, Park View Christian Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Opposes American commerce contributing to Japan’s destruction of China.
subfiles.summary: Beretta Burton joins the appeal, naming Park View Christian Church in Washington.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Grace S. Kifer
subfiles.from: Grace S. Kifer
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Seeks an end to American exports used in Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Grace Kifer's petition condemns violations of international law and attacks on Chinese civilians and asks to stop the trade.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Ruth M. Hirzes
subfiles.from: Ruth M. Hirzes, surname uncertain
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Requests federal measures against American support for Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Ruth Hirzes's petition lists aircraft, shells, scrap iron and oil among American contributions to Japan's war and supports Chinese independence.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Mrs. H. E. La Rue
subfiles.from: Mrs. H. E. La Rue, Takoma Park Baptist Church
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Calls for an end to American trade facilitating Japan’s war against China.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. H. E. La Rue signs the standard petition, noting Takoma Park Baptist Church.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by a member of First Methodist Church
subfiles.from: Petitioner surnamed Hartley, first name unclear
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Asks federal authorities to halt American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: A member of First Methodist Church in Washington endorses the petition condemning Japanese attacks and American exports.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by M. D. Goodwin
subfiles.from: M. D. Goodwin, reading uncertain
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Urges action to end American trade that strengthened Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: M. D. Goodwin's petition says strategic exports make the US complicit and seeks federal measures to stop the traffic.

subfiles.title: Petition signed by Mrs. Adams
subfiles.from: Mrs. Adams, given name unclear
subfiles.to: President of the United States and Congress
subfiles.about: Petitions for an end to American shipments supporting the Japanese invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. Adams signs the final petition, with a possible Tacoma address.
